one_liner: Small zero-copy Rust HTTP/1.x parser; beats picohttpparser only on short requests (1.14-1.29x), ties or loses on realistic ones.
what_it_does: A Rust crate that parses HTTP/1.x request and response heads (request or status line plus header fields) straight from a byte slice without copying. Request::parse(buf, &mut headers) returns Ok(Complete((req, consumed_len))), Ok(Incomplete) when it needs more bytes, or an Error enum (InvalidMethod, InvalidPath, InvalidFieldValue, OutOfCapacity, ...). A parsed request gives you method, target, minor_version and a slice of HeaderField { name, value }, all &str views into your buffer. Headers go into anything that implements HeaderFieldCollection. Impls are provided for Vec and, behind the optional 'arrayvec' feature, for ArrayVec<[_; 16]>. It is not a pico drop-in: there is no C ABI, no chunked decoder and no body handling.
how_it_is_fast: Character classes are 256-entry bool lookup tables (tchar, field-value and reason-phrase), scanned by a hand-unrolled 8-bytes-per-step loop (Scanner::read_while_continue_with), which is the same shape as pico's non-SSE path. Header values alone get an SSE4.2 path. PCMPESTRI (_mm_cmpestri with _SIDD_CMP_RANGES) scans 16-byte blocks for the first byte in 0x00-0x08, 0x0A-0x1F or 0x7F-0xFF, which is the same trick as pico's findchar_fast, and tails under 16 bytes fall back to scalar. Parsing is generic over the header collection and builds &str views with from_utf8_unchecked (sound because the tables admit ASCII only), so it monomorphizes and inlines fully under the bench profile's LTO with codegen-units=1. The README does not say why thhp wins on the short request. In the bench, pico is called over FFI, so its fixed per-call cost weighs more on a 56-byte request, and thhp never uses SIMD for the method, target or header names.
when_to_use: A Rust server or proxy whose traffic is mostly small requests (tens of bytes, a few short headers). On the 56-byte request the README shows 35-37 ns for thhp vs 42-45 ns for picohttpparser (via FFI) and 41 ns for httparse 1.3.
You want a tiny parser to vendor and change: about 1.2k lines including tests, MIT, no runtime dependencies (arrayvec 0.4 is optional), and a simple Complete/Incomplete API over &str slices.

You control the x86-64 build and can pass RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse4.2" (or an equivalent target-cpu). Only with that flag did the ~700-byte browser request reach parity with pico (159 vs 160 ns).
Internal or controlled traffic where a strict ASCII-only policy is acceptable or wanted: control bytes and all bytes >= 0x80 in the target, header values and reason phrase are rejected.
when_not_to_use: Realistic header-heavy browser requests on a default build. Without the explicit SSE4.2 flag, thhp took 198 ns vs pico's 153 ns (pico ~1.29x faster). With the flag, its 0.6% lead sits inside the +/-23 ns and +/-37 ns spreads.

Public-facing traffic that may carry raw UTF-8 or obs-text bytes in paths, cookies or header values. thhp returns InvalidPath or InvalidFieldValue on those, while the pico version it was benchmarked against allows bytes >= 0x80.

You need what pico or httparse provide beyond the head parser: chunked-body decoding, obs-fold continuation lines (rejected as InvalidFieldName), pico's last_len incremental re-check (thhp re-parses from byte 0 on every call), or a C ABI.

Anything that needs upkeep. The last commit and the 0.2.0 release are both from 2018-12-22. No issue or PR was ever filed, crates.io lists 0 reverse dependencies, no rust-version is declared, and the only CI was Travis in 2018.
Non-x86 or no_std targets: they get the scalar table path only (no NEON or AVX2), and no_std mode needs nightly because of #![feature(alloc)].

integration.form: crate (thhp 0.2.0 on crates.io; about 1.2k lines, easy to vendor)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime; optional arrayvec 0.4; build-dependency version_check 0.1
integration.min_toolchain: Not declared. The library targeted stable Rust (2018 Travis matrix: stable/beta/nightly; the last commit dropped the 1.20.0 job). build.rs enables SIMD only on rustc >= 1.27. The code is 2015-edition with crate:: paths, which by inference needs rustc 1.30+. The benches (#![feature(test)]) and no_std mode need nightly. It was not rebuilt on a current rustc.
integration.platforms: Any target for the scalar path. x86/x86-64 builds with the std feature get the SSE4.2 header-value path, chosen at runtime by is_x86_feature_detected!. No NEON or AVX2.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Request::parse and Response::parse are stateless functions over a caller-owned buffer and header collection, and the only statics are const lookup tables.

gotchas: The Vec impl never grows: its capacity is the hard header limit, so Vec::new() fails with OutOfCapacity on the first header. The ArrayVec impl is fixed at 16 headers.

The returned headers slice is the whole collection, and headers pushed before an Incomplete result stay in it. Call headers.clear() before every parse and every retry, as the bench does, or you get stale or duplicate headers.

It is lenient in some places, per the code. An empty method (' / HTTP/1.1'), an empty target ('GET  HTTP/1.1') and an empty header name (':v') all parse successfully. Bare LF line endings are accepted, and header values keep their trailing whitespace. Responses must have a space after the 3-digit status, so 'HTTP/1.1 200\r\n' is rejected with InvalidStatusCode.

The SSE4.2 path covers only header values of 16 bytes or more, with a runtime feature check on each call. find_fast has no #[target_feature(enable = "sse4.2")], so without RUSTFLAGS the PCMPESTRI intrinsic is probably not inlined. That fits the slower 'implicit SSE4.2' full-request result (198 vs 159 ns).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the Rust siblings, httparse is the default pick: it is maintained (last push 2026-06-30), has SSE4.2/AVX2/NEON/SWAR modules and supports no_std on stable. picohttpparser-rs wins only on header-heavy inputs and loses on tiny ones, while thhp is the reverse. Pick thhp only if you want a vendorable parser tuned for small requests (35-37 ns vs httparse 41 ns and pico 42-45 ns in its own 2018 bench); to beat pico in C by real margins, the vkrasnov AVX2 fork or httpp report much larger gains.
verified_claims_summary: These are the author's own cargo +nightly #[bench] results (opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units=1; nightly version, CPU and OS not stated). The baseline is picohttpparser as vendored in picohttpparser-sys 1.0, compiled by the cc crate with -msse4 and called over FFI, with httparse 1.3 as a third contestant. With RUSTFLAGS +sse4.2, the ~700-byte browser request took 159 vs 160 ns (a tie within noise) and the 56-byte request 35 vs 45 ns (~1.29x). With default flags the results were 198 vs 153 ns (pico ~1.29x faster) and 37 vs 42 ns (~1.14x). Each configuration is a single pasted run with no hardware stated and no third-party reproduction.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-12-22 (the date of both the last commit and the 0.2.0 release; 15 stars, ~5,000 all-time downloads, 0 reverse dependencies). It is MIT and small with no runtime dependencies, so it can be vendored, but nothing has built it since its 2018 Travis CI and it was not built for this entry.
